summary: Background discussion for the Telnet proposal in RFC 137. It gives views from committee members about the arguments behind the design, to help implementers interpret and evaluate it. The authors say these are not the committee's agreed position.

eli5.summary: A group wrote rules for a game, and this is a side note explaining why they chose them. It is only some members' thoughts.

subtitle: The reasoning behind the first Telnet proposal: why a standard terminal code, why ESC, and how echo and break are handled.

tldr.problem: Implementers needed to understand why RFC 137 chose its approach, and to judge it before the Atlantic City meetings.
tldr.mechanism: The note explains the arguments: one network-wide intermediate terminal code, ESC as an escape, a no-echo-from-server default with I ECHO and YOU ECHO, and X'80' with an INS to deliver urgent signals.
tldr.outcome: The author says these are his understanding of the arguments, not the committee's agreed view. It updates RFC 137 and the unit metadata lists RFC 158 as a later update.

today: This note updates RFC 137, and the unit metadata lists RFC 158 as a later update to it. Its status is given as unknown.

sections.title: Why a Standard Intermediate Code
sections.content:
A network-wide intermediate representation of terminal code means the using and serving sites need not keep information about each other's terminals. That only works if three things hold: the serving site specifies how the intermediate code maps to its own terminal codes, the user knows that mapping, and the using site lets the user enter all of the intermediate codes and control signals.

A rival idea, that the using site should translate to and from the code the serving site expects, was rejected because every using site would need tables for every serving site, constantly maintained as hosts were added. Because it was unknown how sites would map the standard 7-bit ASCII in an 8-bit field, the user must be able to cause every one of the 128 ASCII codes.

The author stresses that this is a discussion by various committee members, and is not the agreed view of the committee.
sections.eli5: Instead of every kid learning every other kid's secret language, everybody learns one shared language and translates just once.

sections.title: Escape, Line Ends and Data Types
sections.content:
Serving sites are encouraged to map the full ASCII code to their own, so no character is left out that might later matter. For any serving-site character without a one-for-one mapping, the site names an escape string starting with ESC (also called ALT MODE). In the RFC's example, an EBCDIC site asks users to enter ESC followed by C for the cent sign, and a using site that prints ESC as a backslash shows \C.

The network-wide line end is carriage return followed by line feed, translated by both sites as needed. A DATA TYPE byte at the start of a connection chooses the conventions in use: X'A0' for ASCII, X'A1' reserved for transparent 8-bit binary and X'A2' reserved for EBCDIC. If the first byte has its high bit zero, ASCII is assumed, and X'88' returns to control mode.

The use of ESC is a convention for the 7-bit ASCII mode, not a Telnet-wide standard.
sections.eli5: When a computer has a letter nobody else has, it says "press the special key, then C". A first label byte tells what kind of language the rest of the message is in.

sections.title: Echo, Break and Urgent Signals
sections.content:
The starting assumption is that the using site provides any echo and the serving site provides none. This avoids trouble for sites that cannot turn echo off. I ECHO and YOU ECHO let the sites pass echo control to each other. The RFC's example is a password prompt, where the serving site takes control of echo so the password is not printed.

BREAK (ATTN on a 2741) is sent as X'81', with reverse break as X'82'. A break can get stuck behind a clogged input buffer, so the user follows it with an X'80'. The using site's Telnet then asks its NCP to send an INS, which warns the server to look for the X'80'. The server treats X'80' as a sync character, strips it and returns to normal mode. If the X'80' arrives before the INS, a counting scheme keeps the handling right.
sections.eli5: If a phone line is jammed with chatter, you can ring a special bell that makes the other side stop and listen for your urgent message.

sections.title: Minimum Implementations and Open Questions
sections.content:
A minimal using site must let the user send any chosen ASCII string, and only that string, but may ignore and strip control signals from the serving site. A minimal serving site may map just the most important 128 controls and graphics and ignore all control signals. A site that cannot act on an incoming control code can reply with X'87' followed by the code it received.

If an ASCII Telnet connection is lost, the other end should assume the process was quit, aborted or failed. The note also asks whether a protocol like Telnet should add functions such as Hold Output or Kill Print beyond what a local system offers, and if so whether they are network-wide standards. It calls for a mechanism to assign and announce DATA TYPE and control codes.

The endnotes correct RFC 137: X'85' becomes Reserved, receipt of X'88' is answered with a double X'88' if the new data type can be handled, and the using site is assumed to echo if necessary.
sections.eli5: A small, simple version of the system is allowed to ignore the fancy signals, and if the line drops, the other side just assumes you left.
